source.title: In Search of Robust Measures of Generalization
source.authors: G. Dziugaite; Alexandre Drouin; Brady Neal; Nitarshan Rajkumar; Ethan Caballero; Linbo Wang; Ioannis Mitliagkas; Daniel M. Roy

record.file_problem: none; full paper text including appendices is present
record.tranche_reason: The study trains convolutional networks on natural image labels, measures training and held-out error, and tests how width, depth, learning rate, and training set size affect generalization. It conceptually tests parts of V2 and V7 through a different architecture family and measures generalization measures' predictions, rather than directly testing the full original claims.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's own reports of training/test error across training-set-size and width interventions, and its measured sign-error results for generalization measures. Cited results from Jiang et al. and other prior work are excluded. Measures used as predictors are recorded only where their reported outcomes bear on tested claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study directly evaluates V7's magnitude-aware perturbation measure against measured generalization gaps and identifies settings where its rankings fail. Its own width interventions also bear on V2 in a different convolutional architecture: width usually changes the gap negligibly. Prediction accuracy is relevant to V7 because that version explicitly concerns how well a measure ranks generalization gaps.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors argue that averaging can conceal failures and advocate robust evaluation over carefully chosen environment families. Every tested measure has empirical sign-error 1.0 somewhere, while useful performance remains in particular subfamilies. They do not claim to establish causal relationships.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a large-scale empirical protocol inspired by Jiang et al.; trains convolutional Network-in-Network models with SGD to a fixed cross-entropy and training-accuracy threshold, then evaluates generalization measures across hyperparameter interventions. Does not reproduce the versions' specific architectures, interventions, or magnitude-aware perturbation comparison.
record.method_sensitivity: Generalization-measure performance varies with dataset (CIFAR-10 versus SVHN), hyperparameter intervention (training-set size, depth, width, learning rate), environment family and averaging/filtering choices. Many CIFAR-10 depth settings fail; some SVHN-only subfamilies show better robustness. Width changes produce little generalization-error change and most width environments are filtered due to Monte Carlo noise.

fits_no_version.finding: Generalization error generally decreases as training-set size increases; some Frobenius-based measures predict the wrong direction.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger training sets generally reduce these convolutional models' generalization gaps, with predictor failures concentrated in some shallow, narrow settings.

fits_no_version.finding: The detailed SVHN depth-pair and width-pair analysis in Figure 9 concerns pacbayes.orig.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Non-magnitude-aware PAC-Bayes measure robustness depends on the particular depth or width comparison and accompanying hyperparameters.

record.peer_reviewed: 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2020)
record.problems: The paper filters out 300 of 10,000 runs that failed training criteria; Monte Carlo noise filtering discards many environments, leaving only 328 width environments in the main analysis. Width changes produce very small generalization-error differences, limiting conclusions. Some result distributions are presented only in figures; no numerical uncertainty intervals are stated for the central sign-error comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: No more than 60 rows were required. Excluded figure-only per-measure values from Figures 1, 5–11 because the supplied text does not state their individual numeric values and the figure layouts do not provide a reliable textual mapping for every result.

untested.parts: No fixed random-label fitting or natural-label versus random-label held-out comparison.
No one-hidden-layer ReLU experiment, interpolation-threshold sweep, or verified zero-error threshold. Retained width comparisons do not establish the direction of small test-error changes.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison or intervention on local connectivity or initialization.
No optimizer comparison or tuning-budget comparison.
No batch-size intervention or fixed-epoch comparison.

No causal effect of flatness is tested. The record does not establish magnitude-aware flatness's overall superiority to every tested norm- and margin-based alternative. Measures include training-size normalization, and experimental ranges differ from Jiang et al.; worst-case failures alone do not determine the overall correlational tendency.
No memorization-based example selection, removal, or retraining comparison.

missing.what: Split the explicit magnitude-aware depth results into separate rows: good performance for 3 to 4, failure with some signs of robustness for 3 to 6, complete failure for 4 to 5, and inconclusive results for 5 to 6. These distinctions are stated in prose and are needed to avoid pooling opposing outcomes.

Record the prose result that pacbayes.mag.flatness has substantially lower maximum sign-error under the weaker, more averaged environment definition than under the main evaluation. This directly demonstrates dependence on evaluation granularity.
missing.locator: Appendix D.3, Exploring a weaker family of environments

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for these versions. Magnitude-aware flatness is explicitly defined through weight-scaled perturbation tolerance in Appendix C.6.6, so its ranking results directly bear on V7. Figure-only values already declared in rows_left_out are not treated as newly missing results.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or natural-label versus random-label comparison.
No one-hidden-layer ReLU sweep; no explicit test of width beyond the zero-training-error interpolation threshold or a test-error peak.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected architectures.

The study tests magnitude-aware flatness as a predictor across interventions, but does not compare networks selected to have similarly low training loss specifically for their perturbation tolerance or directly test the stated ranking against all norm- and margin-based measures under the exact CIFAR-10/SVHN conditions without augmentation.
No removal of memorized training examples.

rows.subject: fully convolutional Network-in-Network model
rows.stage_stated: trained to cross-entropy 0.01 and training accuracy greater than 99%
rows.operation_detail: Compared generalization error across paired width settings, holding other hyperparameters fixed.

conditions.value: 328 remain after Monte Carlo noise filtering

rows.measure: Generalization error change under width intervention; reported as very small
rows.value: Generalization error changes very little in response to width interventions
rows.note: Width results concern error change and the number of environments surviving noise filtering; the text does not report a direction or size of test-error change sufficient to assess whether test error keeps falling past interpolation.
rows.check: Appendix A.1 explicitly describes width-induced gap changes as often negligible; only 328 of 4,000 width environments survive filtering. This supports absence of an appreciable width effect in many settings, rather than continued improvement. The direction in retained environments is unspecified. Training criteria establish cross-entropy 0.01 and accuracy above 99%, not verified zero training error for every retained run.

rows.value: No measure has average-case performance much better than a coin-flip in CIFAR-10 width environments
rows.locator: Section 6, Comparison to Jiang et al.; Appendix D.2, Figure 10
rows.note: This evaluates predictors of the sign of generalization-error changes, not whether test error itself falls or rises as width increases.
rows.check: The quoted coin-flip comparison concerns CIFAR-10 depth environments, not width. For width, Section 6 instead identifies pacbayes.mag.flatness and two path-norm measures as exceptions with better average performance than most measures. Predictor sign-error does not measure V2's direction of test-error change; replace this row with the correctly attributed measure-specific comparison.

rows.baseline: 0 is perfect prediction; 0.5 is coin-flip sign-error
rows.value: Many measure failures occur in CIFAR-10, where smaller tested networks suffer significant overfitting; robust sign-error is maxed out for every measure across depth interventions
rows.note: This gives a depth-specific negative qualification for the family of measures, including the flatness measures discussed in the surrounding text; it does not directly test weight perturbation tolerance as the version defines it.
rows.check: Section 6 explicitly identifies complete failure of pacbayes.mag.flatness for depth 4 to 5 and maximum depth-family sign-error of 1.0. Restrict the row to those failures; it currently conflates them with successful and inconclusive depth comparisons. Almost all failing environments are CIFAR-10, rather than every depth environment being a failure.

source_check.correct: Separate the depth comparisons: pacbayes.mag.flatness performs well for depth 3 to 4, completely fails for depth 4 to 5, and permits no conclusion for depth 5 to 6. Almost all failing environments are CIFAR-10. Restrict reversed to the explicitly failing comparisons; the current value summarizes failure locations without identifying the reversed comparison.

relation.reason: Its own experiments compare generalization measures with measured generalization-gap changes under controlled hyperparameter interventions.

tranche.reason: The study directly identifies failures of magnitude-aware-flatness predictions and argues that aggregate evaluation conceals conditions requiring qualification.

source_check.notes: Section 5 footnote 4 asserts zero training error; Appendix C specifies cross-entropy 0.01 and training accuracy above 99%, so an exact zero-error acceptance threshold is not documented. The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased; the 90%-subfamily result is not specifically attributed to pacbayes.mag.flatness.
